title: Al-Amin, the trustworthy
hook: a young shepherd and merchant becomes known in Mecca as the one you leave your valuables with

segments.voice: Yesterday, mother, grandfather, uncle: three homes by the age of eight. Your line was someone always took him in. Did you thank one of yours? Day eighty-two.

Think about who you'd hand your house keys to. Not your phone password, your actual house keys, for a month, while you're away. Most of us have a short list. Maybe one or two names. Now picture a whole town with the same name on that list. In Mecca, a young man, still in his twenties, not rich, not powerful, an orphan raised by his uncle, had a nickname everybody used. You met it on day twenty of this path. They called him al-Amin. The trustworthy one. Today, the word behind the nickname.
screen: `WHO GETS YOUR KEYS?` → `ONE NAME ON EVERYONE'S LIST.` → `AL-AMIN.`

segments.voice: The word is amanah: a trust. Something handed to you that isn't yours, that you're expected to keep safe and give back whole. Money left in your care. A secret. A job. A promise. It comes from the root a-m-n, which means to be safe, secure. The same root gives iman, faith, and amin, the trustworthy. So in Arabic, faith, safety and trustworthiness are family. How did he earn the name? Not with speeches. As a boy he herded sheep for Meccan families for a few coins; a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says he told his companions every prophet had been a shepherd. As a young man he traveled with the trade caravans and dealt honestly, when the market ran on clever deals. And the name stuck so hard that, years later, even the people of Mecca who fought him most bitterly kept leaving their valuables with him. The seerah says that on the night he finally left Mecca, he left his cousin 'Ali behind for one reason: to return every one of those deposits to its owner. Even his enemies' things. The Qur'an makes this a command for everyone. In Pickthall's translation: “Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners.” And it goes further. It describes the amanah, the trust, being offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and they shrank from carrying it. And the human being took it on. Muslim scholars read that trust in many ways: our faith, our bodies, our time, the earth itself. Everything we hold is held on loan.
screen: `AMANAH: A TRUST, GIVEN BACK WHOLE.` · `FAITH, SAFETY, TRUST: ONE ROOT.` · `EVEN HIS ENEMIES LEFT THEIR THINGS.` · `RESTORE DEPOSITS TO THEIR OWNERS.` · then, large: `BE THE ONE THEY TRUST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one promise exactly. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you said you'd do. A call you promised. A thing you borrowed. A deadline. An I'll be there at six. Pick one that's still open. Picture keeping it exactly, not roughly, not late, not almost. On time, and whole. Decide when you'll do it today. If you pray, you can ask Allah to make you trustworthy in small things. The bell holds the time.
Amanah. A trust: whatever is placed in your care, to be kept safe and given back whole. The root of al-Amin, the Prophet's name in Mecca.
Your line: be the one they trust. Keep the promise you picked, exactly as you said it. Tomorrow, a businesswoman notices him. Day eighty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims treat keeping trusts, returning loans, keeping secrets and keeping promises as part of faith itself, and a hadith lists betraying a trust among the signs of a hypocrite.
